request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Banquet server, male, 3rd year

Interviewer: How much of the banquet service charge do you frontline staff get?

Interviewee: The service charge is distributed centrally according to hotel regulations. The proportions are determined by management. We on the front line are not involved. There’s a line on the payslip called service bonus. The figure is different every month. How exactly it’s calculated, we don’t really know, and we don’t really need to know. It gets paid every month anyway. Last year a colleague asked once in the group chat what the proportions of the service charge were and whether they could be made public. Later he was moved to the dishwashing room. It was said to be a normal job rotation. Every department has them. After that nobody asked about it in the group chat again. He’s still there now. He’s doing fine. Sometimes we run into each other in the staff corridor and say hello. He talks less than he used to, and he doesn’t say much in the group chat any more. Anyway, the hotel has its regulations. It’s not something for us to think about. We just need to do our own service well. Actually, the benefits here are pretty good overall. Meals and accommodation are included. The dorm rooms are for two people, with air conditioning and a washing machine. It’s much better than the hotel I was at before. There’s also a year-end bonus. Last year it was a month and a half’s pay. Next month is the peak wedding season. Every weekend we’ll have three events, setting up from nine in the morning and clearing the tables until ten at night. Recently we’ve been practising new napkin folds. There’s one called the peacock fan that takes more than twenty folds, and I can already do it pretty quickly. My team leader says I fold better than anyone else in this intake, and I might move up a grade before New Year. If you’re interested, you could come and watch us set up at the weekend. It looks really impressive. Lots of the new people take photos and post them on WeChat Moments.
